b3-price.name: The Price of a Yes
b3-price.region: Merrowgate: the Lantern Hall, the north quay, and the casting pit at the end of the old rope-walk
b3-price.threat: The Lantern Hall is selling castings: a town pays the guild, a volunteer goes into the bronze, and the guild pays the volunteer's family for life. Tonight it casts Merrowgate's own bell, around a docker who owes money.
b3-price.brief: Late summer. The Lantern Hall has painted a price for a casting on a board outside its door. Tonight it casts a ward for Merrowgate itself, around a docker called Coll Garrow, and his daughter will be paid for it every month for the rest of her life.

opening.narrate: Late summer in Merrowgate. The harbour smells of tar and hot stone, and the gulls sit on the bollards with their beaks open in the heat. Up the hill from the quays, on the steps of the Lantern Hall, there is a new board, painted in good blue and gold, the way the guild paints its prices.

A WARD FOR YOUR TOWN. One casting, four hundred gold, paid to the Hall. The volunteer's family paid twelve gold a month by the Hall, for life. Every volunteer asked three times, in private, by a Hall clerk. Enquire within.

There is a queue under it. Reeves' clerks from inland towns with purses on chains. A farmer with his hat in both hands. A woman in a good coat with a list. They wait the way people wait at a chandler's, patiently, as if what they have come to buy is rope.
Sitting on the bottom step, out of the way of the queue, with a satchel on his knees and his coat folded beside him in the heat, is Commander Idris Hesk.

oneOf.narrate: He is out on licence to the Lantern Hall. The law the council wrote over the rite needs a trained caster to read it aloud. Corvane, who did every casting in Vell, will not cast again. Hesk stood at every one of them, and he will.
The Lantern Hall bought his bond from the council's custody in the week the council burned every copy of the rite it could reach. It was a very large bond. The Hall paid it in a morning, in coin.

Merrowgate's harbour court claimed him from the council's custody as a contractor, with the seal on the papers still soft. The council left the rite to each town, and this town wanted someone who could read it.
He is out of the council's custody on papers from Merrowgate's harbour court, with the seal on them still soft.

opening.narrate: He sees you coming up from the quay and does not get up. He does not look surprised. He has the look of a man who has been told where you were every day for a month.

opening.text: I'm not running, if that's what you're wondering. My papers are in order and I'm on the inland coach at noon. The Hall has seven towns waiting for someone who can read the words properly. I'm the someone.
You were in a cell.
I was. Now I'm employed. The council wanted me where it could see me, Stoneward. It can see me. I'm on the steps.

opening.narrate: The Hall's great door opens and a woman comes out into the sun with a ledger under her arm, carried the way other people carry a sleeping child. She is fifty or so, with grey hair cropped short like a sailor's and ink on both cuffs. Guildmistress Cass Ord, of the lantern guilds.

oneOf.narrate: She has run the guilds since Pell Haverick fell at the Vote. People on the quays say she ran them before that, from the second desk, and that Haverick never noticed.
The guilds say Pell Haverick has retired to the country, to a house nobody in Merrowgate has seen. Cass Ord has run the guilds since the Vote, and nobody in Merrowgate has asked her to stop.

opening.text: You'll be the hero of the free wards. I've wanted to meet you since the spring. Come in out of the sun. I'll show you anything you like. I'll show you the ledger.
People think we're hiding something. We're not. It's painted on the board. The poor have always paid for safety. Now somebody pays them.

opening.narrate: Down on the quay, a docker is mending nets on an upturned crate, with a girl beside him gutting fish into a bucket. Everyone going past looks at him. He has his name on a board too, smaller, nailed to the Hall's door: tonight's casting, at the old rope-walk. Coll Garrow, docker, thirty-six.

talks.label: Let Guildmistress Ord show you the ledger

lines.narrate: Cass Ord's office is at the top of the Hall, with a window over the whole harbour. She puts the ledger on the desk between you, opens it, turns it round so it faces you, and sits back with her hands folded.

It is a good ledger, kept in three hands and ruled in red. Each line is a casting: the town; the price, paid; the volunteer's name and age; the family's name, and the sum paid every month, with a tick for every month it has been paid. There are nineteen lines since midsummer. Every tick is there.

lines.text: Kettle Down. Ambry. Ferrin's Mill. Two at Hollowmere, because it's a long valley. I can give you each of their names without the book. I go to every casting myself. Somebody from the Hall should be there who isn't paid to be.

My father lit the lamps on the mole for forty years, at nine coppers a night. The cold got into his chest one winter and he died of it in the spring, and nobody paid my mother anything, because nobody pays the families of the people who keep other people safe. Not the guilds. Not the wards. Not your council.

I pay them. Twelve gold a month, for life. Bett Garrow will be the best-fed girl on the north quay by the winter. Tell me what's wrong with that, and I'll write it down. I mean that. I keep a page for it.
And who decides whether a yes is real?
A Hall clerk asks them three times, alone. If they say yes three times, it's yes. What would you have me do, Sister? Look inside them?
No. I've tried that. It doesn't work as well as people hope.

lines.narrate: She turns to the back of the ledger. The last page is headed, in her own hand, Objections. There are eleven lines on it, each with a date and a name. Some are from reeves. One is from a priest in Ambry. She leaves a space under the last one and holds out the pen to you, and waits, and does not seem to mind how long you take.

talks.label: Sit with Hesk on the Hall steps while he waits for the coach

lines.narrate: Hesk moves his satchel so that you can sit. Close to, he looks older than he did on the Iron Road. Custody has taken some weight off him, and none of the straightness.

lines.text: You beat me on a road. The road was never the argument.

Six hundred and eleven of my people died in their beds, the winter before last, waiting for enough volunteers. I told you that in Vell. It's still true. It'll be true every winter until the free wards decide what they think, and you don't decide quickly, any of you. You decide fairly. It takes a long time to be fair.

The willing are a luxury. I said that in Vell and you looked at me as if I'd spat. They are. A town that can wait for a real yes is a town that can afford to wait. Most can't. The Hall has found a way to make them afford it. I don't love the Hall. I read for whoever will let me read.
You'll stop the casting tonight, if you can. I'd think less of you if you didn't try. I'll be thirty miles inland by then, reading to a reeve in a barn.
And the barn after that. And the one after that.
Yes. Unless someone has a better idea. Have you got one, Stoneward? I've been asking since Vell. Nobody has.

lines.narrate: The coach comes up the hill at noon. He gets on it with his satchel and his coat, and nods to you through the window, as if you had come to see him off.

talks.label: Go down to the north quay, where Coll Garrow is mending nets with his daughter

lines.narrate: Coll Garrow is a docker with a docker's back and big, careful hands, mending nets on an upturned crate because there is no work for him on the quay today. His daughter Bett is ten, and is gutting fish into a bucket beside him, faster than he mends, without looking at what her hands are doing.

lines.text: Tonight. In the pit at the end of the old rope-walk. They're casting the harbour its own bell at last. The Hall says Merrowgate shouldn't only sell them, it should have one. They wanted a docker. I said yes.

Twelve gold a month. Do you know what twelve gold a month is, on the north quay? It's boots. It's a room with a window in it. It's her at the Sallows school with the clerks' children, and not down here with the fish.

lines.narrate: Bett does not stop gutting.

lines.text: He says it's like going to sea. A long trip. You don't come back for a while.
People come back from sea.
Bett.
They do. Mam's brother came back from the whaling. He was gone four years.
He's not going to sea. You know he's not. Has anyone asked you, Bett? Has anyone even—
Nobody needs to ask her. She's ten.

lines.narrate: Coll goes back to the net. His hands have started to shake, and he is making a bad job of the knot, and Bett reaches over without a word, takes the shuttle off him, and ties it herself.

talks.label: Find out what Elske Marrow makes of the Hall

lines.narrate: Elske Marrow holds Merrowgate's seat on the free wards' council. You find her alone in the harbour council's chamber, reading the motion that will be put tomorrow at noon: that paid castings be banned within the city's walls.

lines.text: I'm going to vote against it. You'll want to know why. I'll tell you, because I'd rather be argued with than guessed at.

Ban it here, and the Hall sells it in the inland towns, where there's no council and no clerk and nobody watching. Here I can see the ledger. Here I can make them pay the families. A ban makes us feel clean and sends the trade into the dark.
I built the Single Voice because I thought one good design would hold. I was wrong about the design. I don't think I'm wrong about this. I'd like you to tell me if I am.

lines.narrate: Elske Marrow works at the harbour hospice now, in the long room at the Sallows, as she has since the council let her go. There is a slate on the wall by the door with nineteen chalk marks on it.

lines.text: Nineteen. Volunteers since midsummer. I count the ones whose families come here afterwards, because the families do come here. To sit with someone.
Six streets. All nineteen came from six streets, on the north quay and in the Tanneries. Not one from the hill. I'm sure that's a coincidence. The Hall is sure too.
I built a thing once that took from the people with least and called it safety. I know what it looks like from the inside. It looks like a ledger.

lines.narrate: Elske Marrow is in a cell at Highpass, as the council judged. A letter from her is waiting for you at the harbour master's office, in her small, neat hand, dated before the board on the Hall steps was even painted.

lines.text: They will sell it. Someone always does. When they do, look at who is volunteering, not who is buying. Look at the streets. And look at the debts. A yes costs very little from someone who owes more than they have.

lines.narrate: She has signed it with her name and nothing else. The council took the title.

b3-price.clue: The Lantern Hall buys debts from Merrowgate's moneylenders, cheaply, from the people on the north quay and in the Tanneries who have nothing behind them. Then a Hall clerk comes round with the paper and a kind voice and offers to clear it, all of it, for one yes. Coll Garrow's debt was bought nine days before he put his name down.

investigate.label: Find out who held Coll Garrow's debt, and when it changed hands

success.narrate: The moneylenders of Merrowgate keep their books on Chandlery Row, in narrow rooms over the shops, and most of them are glad to talk about the Lantern Hall, because the Hall has been very good for business.

It buys debts. Not all of them: the ones on the north quay and in the Tanneries, from people with nothing behind them, at a third of what they are worth. Then a Hall clerk goes round with the paper and a kind voice and offers to clear it. All of it. For one yes.

Coll Garrow owed forty-one gold on Chandlery Row, for his wife's last winter: the physician, the coal, the burying. The Hall bought the paper on the ninth of the month. He put his name down for the casting on the eighteenth. The Hall's clerk initialled the page both times.

success.text: Nine days. They bought him, and then they asked him.
And he said yes three times. In private.

failure.narrate: Chandlery Row is glad to talk about the Lantern Hall in general and will not talk about any one name. You learn that the Hall has been buying paper from the moneylenders since the spring. You do not learn whose.

route.label: Push through the harbour crowd to the rail of the casting pit before the reading

success.narrate: By dusk half of Merrowgate is going down to the old rope-walk to see the harbour's own bell cast, and you go with them, and then through them, and you are at the rail of the pit before the casting master has opened his book.

failure.narrate: By dusk half of Merrowgate is going down to the old rope-walk, and you are at the back of it. By the time you reach the rail of the pit the casting master is already on the platform with his book open, and a line of Lantern Hall guards stands across the pit stairs.

direct.label: Walk down to the rope-walk with the rest of the harbour
direct.text: You go down to the old rope-walk with the rest of Merrowgate, at the pace of the crowd, and find a place at the rail where you can see.

approach.narrate: The old rope-walk runs a quarter of a mile along the harbour wall: a long low shed where the guilds once laid rope. At the far end, where the tar-boilers stood, the Hall has dug a pit and lined it with firebrick, and the furnace at the bottom of it has been burning since dawn. You can feel it on your face from the door.

People have come the way they would come to a launching. There are children on their fathers' shoulders. A man is selling hot pies from a tray. A guild band is playing something slow, not well, and the crowd is talking over it.

approach.text: They've come to watch. Of course they have. I'd have come to watch, if I didn't know.

approach.narrate: On the platform over the pit there is a bell-mould the height of a man, and beside it, in a clean shirt, with his hair combed down with water, stands Coll Garrow.

crisis.narrate: The casting master is a Hall man in spectacles, reading from the copy the Hall took out of Vell, word by word, with a clerk holding the lamp for him. Hesk is not here. He read the words through once for the casting master at noon, slowly, and caught the inland coach.

Cass Ord stands at the rail with the ledger open in her arms. She reads Coll's line out to the crowd in a clear voice: his name, his age, his daughter's name, twelve gold a month for life. The crowd claps, the way people clap when a ship goes down the slip.

crisis.text: Coll Garrow. You've been asked three times, in private. I'll ask once in public, because the harbour should hear it. Do you come of your own free will?

crisis.narrate: In the front row, at the rail, Bett Garrow is standing with a bucket of fish she has forgotten to put down. She is not clapping.

At the foot of the pit stairs, a line of the Hall's guards in guild blue has closed up across the steps: hired swords, with truncheons. They are there for the crowd. They have been told that crowds sometimes change their minds.

peaceful.label: Talk Coll down in front of the whole harbour, with the day his debt was bought
peaceful.labelNoLead: Talk Coll down in front of the whole harbour

success.narrate: You do not talk to the crowd. You talk to Coll, across the pit, loud enough for the crowd to hear. You tell him what Chandlery Row told you: forty-one gold, for his wife's last winter, bought by the Hall on the ninth of the month for a third of what it was worth. Nine days before he said yes.

success.text: They said the debt was cleared. As a kindness. After.

success.narrate: You ask Cass Ord, in front of everyone, whether the Hall bought Coll Garrow's paper before he volunteered or after. She does not lie. You can see her decide not to.

success.text: Before. We buy the paper first. It's kinder. Nobody should have to say yes with a lender at the door.

success.narrate: Something goes through the crowd that is not a cheer.

You do not talk to the crowd. You talk to Coll, across the pit. You ask him what he owes, and to whom, and he tells you, because he is an honest man and does not know how not to: forty-one gold on Chandlery Row, for his wife's last winter. Cleared by the Hall. As a kindness.
You ask him when they cleared it: before he said yes, or after. He has to think. The crowd waits while he thinks, and goes quiet while it waits.

success.text: Before. They said I'd want it off my mind.

success.narrate: Then you ask him to look at Bett.

success.text: She's still got the fish. She's still holding the bloody fish.

success.narrate: He comes down off the platform by the ladder at the back. The guards at the stair let him pass, because the whole harbour is watching, and because Cass Ord nods to them to let him. He goes along the rail to his daughter, takes the bucket from her, and holds it, as if that is what he came down for.

success.text: He can come back tomorrow. Most do. And the debt stays cleared, whatever he decides. I'm not a moneylender. Write that on my page too, hero, with the rest.

failure.narrate: You call across the pit to Coll, and a Hall man at the rail calls back louder: here is the free wards' hero, who broke the Single Voice and left the harbour to the lantern guilds, come to tell a docker what his daughter is worth.

The crowd turns the way crowds do, all at once. Somebody shoves. The guards at the stair come down into the crowd with their truncheons out, and Coll is still on the platform, and the casting master has turned the page.

objective.name: Bring Coll down
objective.label: Get Coll Garrow down from the casting platform
objective.description: Four successful actions get you past the Hall's guard on the pit stairs and Coll down from the platform before the reading ends.
objective.failText: The casting master reaches the last page before you reach the platform, and stops there, because Cass Ord has put her hand flat on his book. 'Not with a fight in the pit,' she says. 'Not in my harbour.' Coll comes down the back ladder on her word, not yours, and the whole rope-walk sees it.
objective.successText: You reach the platform with the guards behind you. Coll lets you take his arm, and comes down.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody is hurt at the rope-walk. The furnace burns all night for nothing, and in the morning the Hall lets it go out.

Three of the Hall's guards are carried out of the rope-walk, and a docker with a broken arm, and the guild band's big drum. The furnace burns all night for nothing, and in the morning the Hall lets it go out.

after.narrate: Coll Garrow is sitting on his upturned crate on the north quay the next morning, with Bett asleep against his side and the cleared paper folded in his shirt.

after.text: I'd have done it. You know that. I'd have gone in for her. I'm not sorry I came down. I don't know yet whether I'm glad.

after.narrate: At noon the harbour council sits, with the doors open, because half the north quay has come up the hill to listen. Cass Ord is there with her ledger. The motion is read: that paid castings be banned within Merrowgate's walls.

Elske Marrow, in Merrowgate's chair, says what she told you: that a ban sends the trade inland, where nobody watches. Then she looks at you, and sits down, and waits to hear what the hero of the free wards will say.

The free wards' relief fund has a clerk here too, with the fund's book: the money the wards have put by for rebuilding, most of it promised to Fenmere's lower village. He has done a sum without being asked. The fund could buy every debt the Hall holds on the north quay and in the Tanneries, and burn them. Fenmere would wait a year for its walls.

after.text: Ban me, and I'll sell inland. Rule me, and I'll sell fewer. Buy my paper, and I'll buy other paper. I'm not your enemy, hero. I'm only the person standing where the money is. Tell them which you want, and I'll do it properly.

after.narrate: The harbour council asks you what you would have it do.

decisions.label: Ask the harbour council to ban paid castings in Merrowgate
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Merrowgate bans paid castings. The Hall takes the trade inland, where nobody is watching.

text.narrate: The motion passes, nine votes to four, with the north quay cheering in the doorway.
Elske votes against it, as she said she would, and comes and shakes your hand afterwards, because she said she would do that too.

text.text: Very well. Inland, then.

text.narrate: By the end of the week the board is gone from the Hall steps. The Hall's coaches go out of the east gate full of clerks, with a casting master and a copy of the rite in a locked box. Inland there is no harbour council, and nobody to read the ledger but the Hall.

text.text: Good. Not here. Then we go and find it inland.

decisions.label: Ask for a rule instead: a witness at every casting, and nothing paid to the family
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Every casting in Merrowgate needs a witness the volunteer chooses, and no family is paid for a yes. Fewer castings, and every one of them lawful.

text.narrate: The rule goes into the harbour's book that afternoon, in the council clerk's best hand. No casting in Merrowgate without a witness the volunteer chooses, who is not the Hall's. And no money to the family, ever, from anyone, for a yes.

text.text: Without the money, who'll say yes?
People who mean it. There'll be fewer of them. That's the point.

text.narrate: You tell her: people who mean it. There will be fewer of them.
The board on the Hall steps is painted over by evening. The new one gives the Hall's price and nothing for the family. The queue under it is shorter by half, and quieter.

decisions.label: Have the free wards' relief fund buy the harbour's debts, and clear them
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The fund buys every debt the Hall holds on the quays and burns them. Fenmere's rebuilding goes unpaid for a year.

text.narrate: The fund's clerk buys the Hall's paper that afternoon, every sheet, at what the Hall paid for it, which Cass Ord insists on being exact about. Four hundred and six debts. They burn them on the north quay at dusk in a tar barrel, and the whole quay comes down to watch, and this time nobody is selling pies.
Coll Garrow's sheet goes in with the rest. Bett puts it in herself.
The clerk writes to Fenmere that night. The lower village's walls will wait another year.

text.text: Four hundred families on the quay don't have to choose this winter. And Fenmere waits. Again. I know. I know it's not fair. But Fenmere isn't standing on a platform.

b3-wren.name: Wren's Bell
b3-wren.region: Cinder Fold: the first forge, the pit over the iron lid, and the cold galleries
b3-wren.threat: The iron lid under the first forge is moving, and the nine founders' bells on it have lost their time. Cinder Fold has voted to cast a ward around Wren, the old keeper of the forge-signal, and Wren has said yes.
b3-wren.brief: Autumn. The lid under the first forge is moving and the nine bells ring out of time. The miners' committee has voted to cast Wren, Nessa's old mentor, into a bell at the pit, and Wren has said yes. The Lantern Hall has offered to do it for nothing.

opening.narrate: Autumn comes early to Cinder Fold. The ground is still warm underfoot, as it always is, but the warmth comes and goes now, like a fever, and at night the whole town can hear the bells under the forge.

There are nine of them: the bells the founders cast nine hundred years ago, hung on the iron lid over the shaft at the bottom of the first forge. All anyone's life they have rung on their own, once each at the turn of every hour, one after another, so that the miners in the galleries know the time. This autumn they ring out of time. Three together, then nothing, then one alone at the wrong hour, like tired people talking over each other because none of them can wait their turn.

Under them, the miners say, the lid is moving. Not much. A finger's width in a month. There is a new bright line in the iron where it has shifted, and people go down the stair on purpose to look at it, and come up quiet.

oneOf.narrate: Last winter was mild. The Mother Bell was quieted at the Vote, and the free wards had a soft winter anyway, and in Cinder Fold everyone said they had been lucky. This autumn nobody says it.

Last winter the council recalled the Mother Bell, and the wards held, and nobody in Cinder Fold ever quite believed they would. The miners kept their own watch on the lid all winter. They are keeping it again.

Last winter the Mother Bell held the free wards by asking them, and every bell in Cinder Fold answered it. The miners still talk about the night the hearth bells rang on their own in every house. There has been nothing like it since, and the lid has not stopped moving.

opening.narrate: The miners' committee met last night in the old casting hall, with the doors open. It voted, thirty-one to four, to cast a ward around one of their own at the pit, with the rite the Lantern Hall brought out of Vell. Then it asked the one it wanted, and she said yes.

It is the same committee that tied fourteen times over the cold galleries, until somebody from over the pass opened them for it. It has not tied once since. People in Cinder Fold say that was your doing. Not all of them say it kindly.

Wren is sixty. Her leg is worse: she uses the stick for walking now, not for pointing at people. She has kept the forge-signal and walked the galleries for thirty years, and she has decided that her last work will be to hold them.

The Lantern Hall has a man at the inn, with a letter from Cass Ord. The Hall will cast Wren for nothing: no fee, a casting master sent at the Hall's own cost. Everybody in Cinder Fold understands why. A free casting at the first forge, of the keeper of the forge-signal, would sell a hundred more.
Wren is waiting at her kitchen door with a letter in her hand that has been folded and unfolded until it is soft. You know the handwriting from across the yard. It runs uphill.

opening.text: Reed. Come in. Sit down. No, sit. I've a thing to read you, and I'd like you sitting for it.

opening.narrate: The committee will not cast without Nessa's answer. A year ago she wrote that she would take the forge-signal after Wren, and the miners have it in their minutes. A casting would make that long yes come due tonight.

opening.text: 'Yes, but not yet. I've got a council to keep an eye on, and you're not dead, so you can manage another winter.'
That's the last line. I've read it every night since. I can't, Reed. That's the trouble. I can't manage another winter, not on those stairs. So it's yes now, or it's no, and I need you to say which.
You can't use my letter. That's my letter. I wrote that so you'd—
So I'd what?
So you'd still be here.

opening.narrate: Wren is waiting at her kitchen door, leaning on her stick.

opening.text: Reed. You came. Good. I've a thing to ask, and I'd sooner ask it than write it. I've seen what happens to your letters.
Stand at the pit with me when they cast. I'd like somebody there who knows how I'd want my coat buttoned. That's all. You don't have to say it's right. You only have to stand there.

opening.narrate: Nessa does not answer. Her hand goes to her coat pocket, where there is a letter folded very small, addressed to Wren, that you have seen her carry since the spring. She does not take it out.
Wren is waiting at her kitchen door. She looks past you, down the yard, for somebody who is not there, and then back at you.

opening.text: No Reed. No. Well. You'll do. I've said yes, and I'd like somebody from over the pass to have heard me say it. Somebody who'll tell her I wasn't made to.

talks.label: Sit with Wren in her kitchen, among the maps

lines.narrate: Wren's kitchen is three paces wide and still full of maps. She has been rolling them up one at a time, tying each one with string and labelling it in pencil: north galleries, cold galleries, the old casting floors, the drain under the Highpass road.

lines.text: Thirty years. I know every gallery under this town by the sound it makes when you knock on it. I know where the water comes in in spring. I know which props are lying to you.

And this leg won't do the stairs another winter. I've been told. I've told myself. So I can sit at the top in a chair, and have people come and tell me how the galleries are, kindly, slowly, as if I'd never been down. Or I can hold them. All of them, for as long as the bronze lasts.
I'm not sad about it. Don't look at me like that. I've thought about it longer than you've thought about anything. I'm choosing the work.
You're choosing to be a bell. That isn't work, that's—
It's the only work there is, girl. Holding something up so other people can walk under it. You know that. You've been doing it badly for twenty years.
I have not been doing it badly.
No. You haven't.

lines.narrate: She ties the string on the last map, the drain under the Highpass road, and writes nothing on its label, and puts it on the shelf by the hearth bell.

talks.label: Talk to Agnes Tallis, who chairs the miners' committee

lines.narrate: Agnes Tallis chairs the miners' committee. She is a short, square woman with a pick-scar through one eyebrow, and she has the minutes of last night's meeting in her apron pocket. She takes them out and gives them to you to read without being asked.

lines.text: Thirty-one to four. The four were Wren's own gallery crew. They voted no because they love her, and they said so. Nobody was paid. Nobody was told what to say. We asked her after, with the doors open, and she said yes before I'd finished asking.

So it's fair. I'd like you to know it's fair before you decide whether to tell us we're wrong. People come over the pass and tell us we're wrong, and they're right more often than I like. This time it's fair.
And the Hall's man can take his letter back to Merrowgate. We voted yes to Wren. We didn't vote yes to Cass Ord. They seem to think in Merrowgate that it's the same thing.

lines.narrate: Since the harbour shut its doors to paid castings, the Hall's man says, Cinder Fold is the best customer the Hall could have. He says it to everyone at the inn. Agnes has stopped going to the inn.

talks.label: Find Nessa, who has been interrupting everyone since the gate

lines.narrate: Nessa has spent the day interrupting people. She interrupted Agnes Tallis in the middle of the minutes. She interrupted the Hall's man at the inn. She interrupted Wren twice, and Wren let her. Now she is sitting on the forge wall with Biscuit, not saying anything to anyone.

lines.text: Everyone keeps telling me it's fair. It's fair. The vote's fair. She isn't being made to. I know. I was there when she said it, and she meant it, and I wanted her to be lying so badly that I nearly—

She pulled me out of a drain when I was nine. With a lamp she'd stolen. And no boots. I keep thinking about the boots. It was winter and she gave me hers and walked home in her socks, and I never once asked her if her feet were cold.

I don't know what I'm for, if she's a bell. That's the stupid truth. I've spent my whole life running at things so she'd see. And she'll be down there, and she'll see everything, and I'll never know if she minds.

lines.narrate: Biscuit puts his head on her knee. She does not seem to notice, and then she does, and puts her hand on it, and keeps it there.

talks.label: Answer a miner's boy who wants to know what the hearth bell is for

lines.narrate: Hew is eight, and his father works the north galleries. He has followed you from the inn to the forge and back, carrying the little bronze bell from his family's hearth, because he wants to ask the hero of the free wards something and has not yet worked out how to begin.

lines.text: Every house has one. Ours is on the shelf by the fire. You ring it at night before you bank the fire down. Gran did. Mam does. I do it now, because I'm the eldest.
What's it for?

lines.narrate: You tell him you do not know. Nobody in Cinder Fold knows. It is the one thing the whole town agrees on.

lines.text: Gran said you ring it when you've given something. I asked her what you give. She said she'd forgotten. She said everybody had.
That's a stupid thing to forget.

lines.narrate: He rings it once, there in the street, to show you how. It is a small, clear note. Somewhere under the forge, a long way down, one of the nine answers it, out of time.

b3-wren.clue: The founders' ledger, in the iron box in the vault under the first forge, lists the nine bells the founders cast on the lid, and beside each one the name of the person it was cast around. On its last page there is a tenth mould, drawn and measured and never used. Under it, in the same hand: Not this way. Ask them all.

investigate.label: Read the founders' ledger in the vault under the forge

success.narrate: The founders' ledger lives in an iron box in the vault under the first forge, and the committee keeps the key. Agnes Tallis lets you have it for an hour, and stands in the door while you read, because nobody has opened it in forty years and she would like to know what it says.

It is a builder's book. Nine bells, each with its weight, its metal, and the day it was hung on the lid. Beside each bell a name, in a careful hand. They are not the founders' names. They are the names of the people the bells were cast around.

On the last page there is a tenth. A mould drawn and measured like the others, larger than any of them, with no name beside it. Never used. Under the drawing someone has written five words in the same hand as the rest, and underlined them twice.
Not this way. Ask them all.

success.text: Ask who? Ask them all what?

success.narrate: Nobody in the vault can tell her. But by the morning everyone in Cinder Fold knows that the founders wrote it, and the miners who are for the casting and the miners who are against it are both quoting it.

failure.narrate: The founders' ledger is in an iron box in the vault under the forge, and you get an hour with it. It is a builder's book, all weights and metals and dates, in an old cramped hand. You find the nine bells and lose the thread of the rest. There is a last page you cannot make out. It looks as though someone underlined something on it.

route.label: Go down the gallery stair to the pit with the miners

success.narrate: The stair down to the pit is four hundred steps cut in the rock, slick with the cold that comes up the galleries now. You take it the way the miners do, with a hand on the rope and your weight back, and you are at the bottom with the committee when the lid starts to move.

failure.narrate: Halfway down the gallery stair the cold comes up the rock all at once, and the rope goes white under your hands, and your fingers stop working on it. You come down the last hundred steps more by falling than climbing, and reach the bottom bruised all down one side.

direct.label: Take the slow way down, by the old ore lift
direct.text: You take the old ore lift down to the pit. It is slow and loud, and it gets you there.

approach.narrate: The pit is the bottom of the first forge: a round chamber cut in the living rock, with the iron lid set in its floor like the cover of a well forty feet across. Around it the nine founders' bells hang on their iron frames, each as tall as a cart. The miners have hung lamps all round the walls. The bright line in the iron, where the lid has shifted, is the width of a hand now.

The mould for Wren's bell is already standing at the edge of the lid, on blocks, where the Hall's casting master will want it. Wren is sitting on a crate beside it with her stick across her knees, watching the bells.

approach.text: Listen to them. They can't keep time. They always did, all my life. You could set a watch by them in the galleries.

crisis.narrate: The lid heaves. It is less a sound than a feeling in the floor, as if the whole mountain has taken a breath. The bright line in the iron opens to the width of an arm, and cold comes up out of it: not the cold of a cellar, but the white cold of the Gloam, which takes the warmth out of what it touches and the memory out of what it takes.

The nine ring all at once, and then not at all. Up the cold galleries, from the mouths along the chamber wall, the white comes in like a tide, and there are shapes in it. They are made of what Cinder Fold has forgotten: the names of galleries nobody walks any more, a song the miners used to sing on the ore lift, a face from a burial nobody went to. The largest of them reaches for the lid like a hand.

crisis.text: Ropes! Every rope! Get them ringing!

crisis.narrate: The miners run for the bell-ropes, two and three to a bell, but the nine will not ring together. Each crew rings in its own time, as it always has, and the bells fight each other, and the white comes on.

crisis.text: They don't know when. Somebody has to tell them when.

peaceful.label: Get the nine ringing in time again, with every miner on a rope, and call the beat
peaceful.labelNoLead: Get the nine ringing in time again, with every miner on a rope

success.narrate: Not this way. Ask them all. You understand it standing there, with the white coming up the galleries: not nine crews ringing nine bells. Everyone. Every miner in the chamber on a rope, and the nine as one bell, the way the founders drew a tenth.
You put every miner in the chamber on a rope. Not only the crews: everyone, two and three to a rope, the committee, the lamp-boys, Agnes Tallis with her apron tied back.
And you call the beat. You stand at the edge of the lid with the cold coming up past you and count out loud, slowly, the way you would count for people learning a dance. One. Two. Pull.

success.text: One, two, pull! Wren, tell them, they'll listen to you!
Pull! On the count! The lot of you, pull!

success.narrate: The first pull is ragged. The second is less so. On the fourth the nine ring together, one great note, and the white in the gallery mouths stops where it is, as if it had been called by name.

You keep counting. You count for an hour. The miners pull until their hands are raw, and change places, and pull again, and the nine ring in time, and the white goes back down the cold galleries the way it came, slowly, and the Gloam's hand sinks back into the line in the lid.
The line in the iron is still there. It is no wider.

failure.narrate: You call the beat, but the crews have rung their own bells their whole lives, and the white is in the chamber, and nobody can hear you over the nine. The ropes go slack in the cold. The Gloam's hand comes up out of the line in the lid, and the shapes come out of the gallery mouths, and there is nothing left to do but fight them in the lamplight.

objective.name: Keep the ropes manned
objective.label: Hold the bell-ropes while the miners find the time
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the shapes off the bell-ropes long enough for the miners to bring the nine back into time.
objective.failText: The shapes reach the ropes on the far side of the lid. Two of the nine go silent, and the miners on them come away grey to the elbow and cannot say their own children's names until the morning. The white goes back down in the end, when the rest of the nine find their time. It goes slowly, and it takes something with it.
objective.successText: The ropes stay manned. The nine find their time, one after another, and the white goes back down the galleries.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody is lost in the pit. The miners come up the stair at dawn with raw hands, and the town is waiting at the top with bread.
Two miners are carried up the stair at dawn, grey to the elbow. They have lost a day, and the names of things they had as children, and they will not get either back.

after.narrate: The nine are ringing in time again. They will not stay in time. Everyone in the pit could hear it: how tired they are, and how near the next heave is. The miners say a month. Agnes Tallis says less.

The committee meets at noon at the edge of the lid, standing, because nobody wants to sit down. The Hall's man from the inn is there with his letter. Wren is there in her coat, with her stick, beside the mould.

after.text: The founders wrote 'not this way'. I've had it in my head all night. Ask them all. And I don't know what it means, and Wren's sixty, and the lid is moving.
It means they couldn't, whatever it was. So they did this instead. And it held nine hundred years. I'll take nine hundred years.
I've said yes. The committee's said yes. The only one in this pit who hasn't said anything is you.
And you, Reed. You've a long yes owing. It's due.

after.narrate: The Hall's man clears his throat and says that the casting master can be here by tomorrow night, at no cost, if the committee will let the Hall say so afterwards.

after.text: We'll pay. Whatever it costs. Then it's ours, and nobody paints it on a board.

after.narrate: There is one more thing, and you are the only one in the pit who can say it. Under Vell, under the iron vault, there is a door, and somebody has opened it and gone down a stair nobody built. Whatever is under the first forge, under the founders' bells and the lid, there may be a way to it from below. Nobody knows yet what is down there. You could ask Cinder Fold to wait one season while you find out.

decisions.label: Let Cinder Fold cast Wren, as she and the committee have chosen
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Wren is cast at the pit, and Cinder Fold holds for a generation.

text.narrate: You tell the committee that it is theirs, and Wren's, and that you will not stand in the way of either.

text.text: Good. That's all I wanted. Somebody to say it out loud.

text.narrate: The committee pays the Hall's casting master his fee in full, in silver, counted out on the lid, and he reads the words the next night by the light of the miners' lamps, and goes home without his supper. The Hall's man never gets his notice painted.
Wren buttons her coat to the neck. She gives her stick to Hew, who has followed everyone down the stair again, and walks to the mould without it.

text.text: It was hers. She chose it. I'm not going to say anything else. It was hers.

text.narrate: In the morning there are ten bells round the lid. The tenth is small and plain, and rings a little ahead of the others, as if it is impatient with them. The nine keep time with it.

decisions.label: Refuse the committee: you will not let them cast her
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You overrule a fair vote. Wren lives. The lower galleries are closed and lost, and twenty families lose their work.

text.narrate: You tell the committee no. Not this way, the founders wrote, and you will not let it be done this way either. You say it in front of everyone at the edge of the lid, and you watch Agnes Tallis's face close like a door.

text.text: It was a fair vote.
I know. I know it was. I don't care. She's not going in.
You've no right. Either of you. It was mine to give.
You've no right. It was mine to give.

text.narrate: The committee closes the lower galleries that week. Without a ward the nine cannot hold them, and the white is in them now and does not leave. Twenty families worked the lower galleries. They go down to the casting hall to be told there is no more work, and some of them look at you on the way out, and some of them do not.

Within the month the Lantern Hall has a new board on its steps in Merrowgate, painted in blue and gold, about the hero of the free wards who overruled a town's fair vote and shut its mine. It brings in a great deal of business.
Wren is angry for a long time. She is alive for all of it.

decisions.label: Ask Wren to wait one season, while you find out what is under Vell
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Wren waits one season. The miners ring the nine by hand all winter.

text.narrate: You ask Wren for one season. Under Vell there is a stair nobody built, going down, and the founders' bells are at the top of whatever it goes down to. If there is another way, the one the founders meant when they wrote ask them all, it may be down there.

text.text: One season. I'm sixty, and you want a season.

All right. One. And I'll tell you now what it'll cost, so you can't say I didn't. Somebody'll be on those ropes every hour of every night all winter, because the nine can't keep time on their own. Somebody'll slip. Ropes are like that.
Then we'll ring them. By hand. All of us, in turns.

text.narrate: They make a roster that afternoon on the casting hall wall: every house in Cinder Fold, an hour each. Wren's name is at the top. She crosses it out and writes it again lower down, among the night hours.

text.text: One season. That's a yes but not yet. That's my one. You've stolen my one.

b3-order.name: The Order
b3-order.region: Saltwick's roof folk, wherever they are living now, and the lamp-store where they are holding Captain Varn
b3-order.threat: Captain Odell Varn, who ordered his hired company out of Saltwick eight years ago and left the town to the tide, has been caught recruiting Saltwick's people for Commander Hesk. The roof council will try him, and Hesk's hired men would rather it did not.
b3-order.brief: Autumn. Orin's old captain, Odell Varn, has been caught among Saltwick's people, recruiting for Hesk and paying in lamp oil. The roof council will try him. Orin means to be in the room.

oneOf.narrate: Autumn. Saltwick is not in Saltwick any more, and Vell is not in Vell. Saltwick's three hundred are camped where Vell's people are camped, on the Highpass road above the pass, on a shelf of rock joined to the road by a plank bridge over a gully. They chose the shelf because it was high. They have run planks along it between the tents, and the children walk the planks rather than the ground.

Autumn. Saltwick is not in Saltwick any more. Its three hundred people live in a quarter of Vell they were given in the spring, four streets by the east wall, and out of habit they have laid planks between the roofs there too. The children walk to school along the planks rather than the street.

Autumn on the Iron Road. Saltwick is still on its roofs. The mist still lies in its lanes to the height of a man, and the lamps still burn on every corner all night, and the planks between the eaves have been relashed so often this year that the rope on them is new from end to end.

opening.narrate: Mags Peller meets you at the ladder, as she did in the spring. She has not changed, except for a new line between her eyebrows, and this time she does not hold the end of her lamp-hook down to anyone.

opening.text: You'll have heard, or you'd not be here. We've got Varn.

opening.narrate: Captain Odell Varn, who commanded the hired road company that left Saltwick to the tide eight years ago, was caught last week recruiting among Saltwick's people for Commander Hesk. He was paying in lamp oil: a cask for a family, and a name for the cask. When they caught him he gave his own name. He did not run.

opening.text: The roof council will try him. Tomorrow, at noon. We've never tried anybody. We've never had anybody worth the trouble.
Where is he?

oneOf.text: The lamp wagon, at the end of the shelf, where we keep the oil. He's tied with a round turn and two half-hitches and a stopper on the tail. The lamplighters insisted.
The cooper's shed by the east wall, where we keep the oil. He's tied with a round turn and two half-hitches and a stopper on the tail. The lamplighters insisted.
The chandler's loft, where we keep the oil. He's tied with a round turn and two half-hitches and a stopper on the tail. The lamplighters insisted.

oneOf.narrate: The lamp-store is a wagon at the far end of the shelf, with its wheels chocked, and a plank running out to its tailboard.
The lamp-store is a cooper's shed by the east wall, with its door on the roof, and a plank running to it.
The lamp-store is the chandler's loft, at the end of a long plank across Cooper's Lane.

opening.narrate: Orin does not say anything. He goes to the edge of the planks and looks along them at the lamp-store's door, and stands there.

talks.label: Go and see Varn in the lamp-store

lines.narrate: Odell Varn is sixty, and sits on an oil cask with his hands tied in front of him and his back straight, as if the cask were a chair at the head of a table. He has a soldier's grey moustache and a soldier's way of looking at a door before he looks at whoever came through it.

lines.text: Stoneward.
Captain.
Not any more. Nobody's captain. I was a captain once, of forty men, for one season, and I brought thirty-nine of them home. You'll want me to say I'm sorry. I'm not. I'd give the order again.

The tide came up that valley like a door opening. Forty men with carts and no bell, against that? We'd have died in the lanes, every one of us, and Saltwick would have died anyway, a quarter of an hour later. I took my company out. That's what a captain is for. I've slept every night since.

And now I go round the families with a cask of oil and offer them a better death than the one I left them to. Hesk's company. A clean yes, the bronze, and your name kept. That's better than the white in the lanes. I'd want it, in their place.
You'd want it.
I'd want somebody to offer. Nobody offered them anything that night. I'm offering.

lines.narrate: He looks at the door again, though nobody is coming through it.

talks.label: Walk the evening lamp round with Mags

lines.narrate: Mags walks the evening lamp round the way she always has, fast, talking, with the dip-stick behind her ear. She does not stop to talk to you. You walk with her.

lines.text: He came here in a good coat, with oil. In the spring we'd hardly any, and he knew it, and he came with oil. Seven families took a cask before anyone thought to ask whose it was.
And they're the families, you understand? The ones from that night. The Heddles. The Ashby boys. Old Corran's widow. He's going round the people he left, with a cask, offering them the bronze.
Your friend's going to ask to be tried with him, isn't he. I can see it on him.

lines.narrate: She lights the next lamp with one turn of the hook, checks it, and goes on.

lines.text: I said I'd think about it, in the spring. I've thought about very little else. I've decided. I'll say it in the room, tomorrow, where everybody can hear. Not out here to you. That wouldn't be fair on anyone.

talks.label: Talk to Davin, who wants to sit on the jury

lines.narrate: Davin Peller is fifteen now, taller than his grandmother, and still has her hands. He has put his name down for the roof council's jury on the slate by the ladder, in letters a hand high. Somebody has rubbed it off. He has written it again.

lines.text: Gran says I'm too young. I'm fifteen. I've lit lamps since I was nine. I put my name down for the wall in Vell in the spring, and nobody said I was too young for that until Gran rubbed it off.

And I don't remember that night. That's the point. Everybody on the council remembers it. I'm the only one who doesn't. Shouldn't there be one person deciding who isn't deciding about their own worst night?
I remember the bell-man's dog. That's all. It got up on the well-house roof and wouldn't come down.
That's a really good argument. That's annoyingly good.
I know. I've been practising it on the hens.

b3-order.clue: Varn has not recruited at random. Every family he offered oil to lost someone the night his company left Saltwick. He is trying to pay a debt with their lives: to give the families he left behind what he thinks is a better ending, and himself a reason for having lived.

investigate.label: Find out which families Varn went to with his oil

success.narrate: Varn's casks are marked, each with a chalk number, and the families who took them still have them, half full, in their kitchens. You go round them. Seven casks. Seven families.

Every one of them lost someone the night the hired company went up the ridge. The Heddles lost a grandmother. The Ashby boys lost their father. Old Corran's widow lost Corran. Peg Halloran, who keeps the town's book of that night, shows you the fourteen names, and seven of them have a cask beside them now, on a list in Varn's hand that he did not know anybody had found.
He has not gone to anyone else in Saltwick. Only to them.

success.text: He's paying them back. That's what he thinks he's doing. Paying them back with the only thing he's got, which is a way to die.

failure.narrate: You go round the families who took Varn's oil, and they shut their doors on you, politely, the way people do when they are ashamed of something and would rather not be asked about it. You count seven casks. You do not find out what the seven have in common.

route.label: Keep watch on the planks through the night before the trial

success.narrate: You take the night watch on the planks with the lamplighters, and an hour before dawn you see them: twelve men in dark coats coming up the far ladders, quietly, with a coil of rope each. You are on the plank by the lamp-store before they are.

failure.narrate: You take the night watch on the planks, and in the dark the long plank is wet, and you go off it, and catch the edge, and hang there over the drop until two lamplighters haul you up. By the time you are back on your feet there are men in dark coats on the far ladders.

direct.label: Sit down outside the lamp-store door and wait for whoever comes
direct.text: You sit down on the plank outside the lamp-store, with your back against the door, and wait for whoever comes for Varn.

approach.narrate: Morning on the day of the trial. The roof council has set out the trial ground on the widest roof it has, the way Saltwick sets out a wedding: benches in rows, a table at the end, and a lamp lit in daylight, because the council thought there ought to be one.
Varn is to be brought along the plank from the lamp-store at noon. Orin has been standing on that plank since first light.
Varn is to be brought along the plank from the lamp-store at noon. Mags has put two lamplighters on that plank since first light.

crisis.narrate: They come at mid-morning: twelve men in dark coats, hired swords, not Commandery, with Lantern Hall money in their purses and a coil of rope each. They come up the far ladders and along the planks fast, the way men walk who have been paid to walk somewhere, and stop at the end of the plank that runs to the lamp-store.

crisis.text: We've come for the captain. Commander Hesk has a use for him, and he's worth more on the Iron Road than in a roof court. Nobody needs hurting. Stand aside and we'll be off your roofs in five minutes.

crisis.narrate: Orin is standing in the middle of the plank, between them and the lamp-store door, with his shield on his arm and his feet set. He has not moved since dawn. He does not move now.

crisis.text: Stoneward, isn't it? You were his. You walked out of here with him. Why do you care if he walks out again?
Because he's going to stand there and be tried, and so am I. Nobody walks off this roof. Not this time.

crisis.narrate: Between them and the lamp-store door there is one plank, and you, and two lamplighters with hooks who have never fought anyone in their lives.

peaceful.label: Stand on the plank with Orin, and make the hired men turn round

success.narrate: You walk out onto the plank and stand beside Orin. You do not draw. Neither does he. You stand there, the two of you, on six inches of board, and look at the twelve.
You walk out onto the middle of the plank and stand there. You do not draw. You look at the twelve.

And you tell them whose roofs these are. You give them the names: the seven of the fourteen, the families Varn went to with his oil, and you tell them that every family here knows by now why the captain chose them. If the hired men take him off the roofs before the trial, they will be carrying him past those families, and every one of them is watching from the eaves.
And you tell them what they know already: that there are three hundred people on these roofs, every one of them watching from the eaves, and that the hired men were paid for a quiet job.

success.text: The Commander said it'd be quiet.

success.narrate: Behind you the lamp-store door opens. Varn is standing in it with his hands still tied, looking at the hired men the way he looks at a door.

success.text: Go home, Sergeant. Tell the Commander I'll come when I'm tried, if they let me. I walked off these roofs once. I'm not being carried off them.

success.narrate: The sergeant looks at the plank, and at who is on it, and at the eaves full of faces, and does the sum the way hired men do. They go back the way they came.

failure.narrate: The sergeant does the sum the other way. 'There's twelve of us,' he says, 'and it's a plank.' He draws, and the hired men come along the boards at you in a line.

objective.name: Hold the plank
objective.label: Hold the plank to the lamp-store
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the hired men off the plank to the lamp-store, so that Varn is still there to be tried at noon.
objective.failText: Two of the hired men get round by the far eaves and cut the lamp-store's lashings, and the plank drops at one end, and for a moment Varn is hanging by his tied hands from the door frame. Davin is the one who reaches him. Varn is tried at noon with a cut across his face and Davin's coat round his shoulders.
objective.successText: The last of the hired men goes back down the far ladder. The plank to the lamp-store is still there, and so is Varn.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody falls. The hired men are gone by noon, back down the Iron Road, and the roof council sits on time.
Two of the hired men went off the planks in the fight, and one lamplighter, and all three were pulled out alive, the lamplighter swearing. The roof council sits an hour late.

after.narrate: Peg Halloran is eighty-one, and has kept the town's book of that night for eight years. She reads out the fourteen names. Then she reads the charge: that Odell Varn came back to Saltwick with Commander Hesk's oil, and offered the families he left behind a cask each for a yes.
Seven families on the benches hear their dead read out beside a cask of oil, and know now why they were chosen.

after.text: I did. I'd do it again. And I'd give the order again, that night. You'll want me to say otherwise, and I won't.

after.narrate: Then Orin stands up from the bench at the back, where he has been sitting since the plank.

after.text: I was at the back of his column with the lantern. I held it up so the carts could see. I held it up so you could see us go. If you're trying him for that night, you're trying me. Try us together.

after.narrate: Nobody on the benches says anything. Davin, at the end of the jury bench, where Peg Halloran let him sit in the end because she said his argument was a good one, looks at his grandmother.

after.text: I'll say one thing before you decide. Then I'll sit down.

Stoneward asked me a question in the spring, on the Vell road, and I told him I'd think about it. I have. Here it is. I'll not forgive a man who's been let off. If this council lets either of them off, it'll be the council I'm forgiving, and the council never did anything to me.

Stoneward's friends heard me say in the spring that I'd think about it. I have. Here it is. I'll not forgive a man who's been let off. If this council lets him off, it'll be the council I'm forgiving, and the council never did anything to me.
That's all. It's not advice. It's only what's true for me.

after.narrate: Peg Halloran looks at you. The roof council has never tried anybody. It would like to know what the hero of the free wards thinks is just.

decisions.label: Argue that both men be tried, and given the same
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Orin and Varn are tried together and given the same sentence: lamp duty for a season. The families think Varn got off lightly.

text.narrate: You argue for it. Orin asked. It was the same night, the same column, the same lantern. The council argues for two hours, and then it gives it.

text.text: Odell Varn. Orin Stoneward. You'll each walk Saltwick's lamps for a season, every night, with a hook, wherever Saltwick is. You'll come when your business under Vell is done, and not before. Saltwick can wait for its lamplighters. It's waited for worse.

text.narrate: The benches are quiet. Then someone at the back says, not loudly, that it is the same for the man who gave the order and the man who held the lantern; and someone else says it is lamps, only lamps, for fourteen; and the quiet goes sour.

text.text: He left a town to die and he gets the same lamps as you?
Yes. That's what I asked for.

text.narrate: Varn bows to the council, stiffly, a soldier's bow. Orin does not bow. He stands there and lets them look at him.

decisions.label: Argue that Varn alone be tried: the captain gave the order, the soldier did not
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Saltwick judges Varn alone and exiles him to the Iron Road. Saltwick is satisfied.

text.narrate: You argue that it was Varn's order. A captain gives an order, and the soldier at the back with the lantern obeys it, or is left on the road himself. The council agrees with you quickly. It is what Saltwick wanted to hear.

text.text: Odell Varn. You'll leave Saltwick by the Iron Road tomorrow, and you'll not come back to it, wherever it is. Your casks go to the families. Your name goes in the book with the fourteen, at the bottom, in red.
That's fair. That's more than fair. I'd have hanged me.

text.narrate: The benches are satisfied, the way people are when something heavy has been put down. Somebody claps.

text.text: I asked to be tried.
You were, Stoneward. We found for you. Sit down.

text.narrate: He sits down. He sits very still, the way he sat on the salt-hall roof in the spring, with his hands hanging between his knees. He has been let off, and he will have to live with it.

decisions.label: Argue that neither man be judged, and send Varn back to Hesk with a message
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Varn goes free, back to Hesk's company, with a message from Orin. Neither Orin nor Maren likes it.

text.narrate: You argue that this council cannot try that night: that a town on its roofs is not a court, that eight years is too long, that neither exile nor lamps will bring back one of the fourteen. And that a man inside Hesk's company who owes Saltwick something may be worth more than a man on the Iron Road who owes it nothing.
The council does not like it. It agrees in the end, the way tired people agree, because nobody has a better idea and the lamps want lighting.

text.text: Then take Hesk a message from me, Captain. Tell his volunteers what you told me in the lamp-store. Tell them what you left. And when they ask you what the bronze is like, tell them you don't know, because you never went to find out.
I'll tell them.

text.narrate: Varn asks whether there is anything you would like him to tell the Commander's volunteers. You tell him to tell them the truth about that night. He says he will.
He goes down the ladder with his hands untied and his casks left behind, and walks off up the Iron Road towards wherever Hesk is, without looking back, the way he went eight years ago.

text.text: That wasn't mercy. I'd like to be clear about that. Whatever that was, it wasn't mercy.

b3-ashford.name: The Town That Said No
b3-ashford.region: Ashford Crossing: the old wall, the bridge, and the lower town by the fulling mill
b3-ashford.threat: Ashford has voted to refuse everything: no casting, no buying one, no giving one of its own. The Gloam is coming up the valley, and the Lantern Hall's recruiters are waiting at the north gate.
b3-ashford.brief: Late autumn. Ashford's town meeting has voted to refuse every answer on offer: no casting, no buying, no giving. The white is four miles down the valley and coming. Reeve Hollis Brede does not intend to change her mind.

opening.narrate: Late autumn. Ashford Crossing sits where the three roads meet the river, and this autumn every road into it has someone on it going the other way.

A month ago Ashford's town meeting voted, in the market hall, three hundred hands to nine. No casting in Ashford. No buying a casting from anyone. No giving one of their own, at any price, to anybody. The motion is painted on a board at the end of the bridge, in plain black, by someone who did not own any blue or gold.
WE WILL NOT BE A MARKET AND WE WILL NOT BE A SACRIFICE.

Reeve Hollis Brede wrote it. She is fifty-five, grey and heavy-shouldered, a miller's widow who became reeve because nobody else would stand, and has been chosen again four times for the same reason. She meets you on the bridge with her arms folded.

opening.text: You'll have come to tell us we're wrong. Everyone does. The Hall's men came to tell us we're wrong at a price. The council sent a letter to tell us we're wrong for nothing. Go on. I've until dark.

opening.narrate: Down the valley to the south, where the river comes out of the hills, the white is lying in the fields like snow that has not fallen. It was ten miles off a week ago. It is four miles off now.

And at the north gate, at a trestle table under an awning, there are recruiters: three Lantern Hall men with a ledger and a cart, and on the cart, under canvas, a bell-mould and a casting master's box. They are not doing much business. They are patient.
Since Merrowgate banned paid castings, the Hall sells inland. Ashford is the first big town inland.
Quartermaster Iona is on the bridge too, a step behind the reeve, with a ledger of her own under her arm. She nods to you the way she nods to a contract she has read before.

talks.label: Ask Reeve Brede why Ashford said no

lines.narrate: Brede walks you along the old wall. It is thick and very old, with trees growing out of it in places, because nobody has needed it for three hundred years.

lines.text: You want to know why. I'll tell you. Not because I think you'll agree. Because I'd like to have said it once to somebody who could do something about it.

Every answer anyone's brought us since the spring has a price on it. The Hall sells you a bell with a person in it. The Commandery took them by quota. The council would vote you one, and then you'd have to find a volunteer, and you know who volunteers. The ones with debts. The ones with daughters. We've seen the Hall's ledger. We've seen whose names are in it.
So we said no to all of it. Not because we're braver than anyone. Because if we say yes to one of them, we've agreed there's a price for a person, and after that we're only arguing about the sum.
And yes, I know what's coming up the valley. I'm not a fool. I'm stubborn. My husband used to say they were the same thing. He was wrong about that too.
Don't try to persuade me. Nobody persuades me. If I change my mind, I'll do it myself, and I'll tell you how I did it.

talks.label: Go through the numbers with Iona, who has priced the walls

lines.narrate: Iona has a table in the toll-house on the bridge, and on it a plan of the old wall, and a ledger with every stretch of it priced.

lines.text: I've priced the walls. Of course I have. Somebody had to. Three hundred years old, built against spears, and the trees in them are holding half of it up.

Inside the walls, in the upper town, there are four thousand one hundred people. Food for the winter, if nobody is greedy and the mill keeps turning. Wood for the winter, no. Not unless we burn somebody's roof.

Outside the walls, in the lower town, eleven hundred people. Houses, a tannery, the fulling mill, the best fields in the valley. None of it can be walled in a month. I've done the sum four times. It comes out the same every time.
I'm not telling her she's wrong. I'm telling her what it costs. She knew already. She asked me to write it down anyway, so that it would be written down.
And I've the carts. Eleven, with drivers. If it comes to moving people, tell me first, not last.

talks.label: Visit Sister Ilse at the archive, where Sable's books went

lines.narrate: The Ashford archive is in the toll-house cellars, dry now, years after the drowning, with Sister Ilse at a desk at the foot of the stairs. Sable's books came here in the spring, in crates.

lines.text: He wrote in all of them. Every margin. I've read them twice. Most of it is a clever man being clever. But at the back of one of the old keepers' books there's a note in his hand from years ago, before Briarwatch, before any of it. 'The first keepers gave a little, each of them. Why did they stop?' He never answered it. I don't think he could.
And there's a note in the front of the first one that isn't his. Yours. I've read it more often than anything of his.
Every note about bells and binding was cut out before they came. I can see where: the pages are like windows. What's left in the margins is mostly about birds. He was very good on birds.
They came as they were, and nobody had read them first, I'm told. I've got through eleven. There's a great deal in the margins, and none of it is kind.

Reeve Brede came down here a week ago and asked me what the archive had on the last time Ashford refused anything. I found her the old wall's building rolls. She sat up all night with them, and came out in the morning looking like somebody had died. I suppose somebody had, three hundred years ago.

talks.label: Talk to the recruiter at the north gate

lines.narrate: The recruiter at the trestle table is a man called Saul Pruett, forty, with a clerk's soft hands and a farmer's sunburn. He offers you a stool and a cup of something hot from a flask, and does not try to sell you anything.

lines.text: I'm from Hollowmere, two valleys over. The Hall cast a man there in the summer. Our miller. The valley's held since; the white hasn't been past the bridge. So when the Hall wanted men who'd seen it work, to go round the towns, I said yes. It's a job. It pays. And I've seen it work.

I'm not here to drag anybody. The reeve's said no, and I've told her I'll not set foot past this gate without her leave, and I won't. I'm here if anyone wants to come and ask. One man has. Twice. I sent him home both times to think about it.

Ansel Wick. He lives in the lower town, by the fulling mill. He's seventy, his wife's dead, and his house is the first one the white will reach. He says he'd rather be the reason it stops than the first house it takes. I can't tell him he's wrong. I've tried.
And when you tried, what did he say?
He asked me if I'd ever wanted anything as much as that. I said no. He said then I should stop arguing with him.

b3-ashford.clue: Ashford's old wall was built the last time Ashford refused, three hundred years ago, when the white came up the valley and the town would not give what the keepers of that time asked of it. The town held. It held by giving up the lower town: every street and field outside the wall went to the white, and Ashford built them all again afterwards, in the same place, and forgot.

investigate.label: Read the old wall's building rolls, and walk its line

success.narrate: Sister Ilse has the building rolls of the old wall in the archive: six skins of parchment stitched together, three hundred years old. Brede has read them. You read them too, and then you walk the line of the wall with them in your hand, down through the lower town, the way it was walked when it was built.

The wall was built in one autumn. The rolls say why. The white came up the valley, and the keepers of that time asked Ashford for something, and Ashford would not give it. The rolls do not say what was asked. They say only that the town refused, and built the wall instead.
Then a list: the streets outside the wall, by name. The fields. The mill that stood where the fulling mill stands now. Beside each one, a single word, in the same hand. Given.

You stand in the lower town with the roll in your hand and you can see it. The ground slopes; the old foundations are there under the new houses. Ashford held, three hundred years ago, by giving up everything outside the wall. Then it built it all again in the same place, and forgot.

success.text: They did my sum. Three hundred years ago. Somebody did my exact sum, and wrote down the answer, and we built on top of it.

failure.narrate: The building rolls are six skins of old parchment in a hand you can barely read. You get as far as the wall being built in a single autumn, three hundred years ago, against the white. You walk its line through the lower town, and lose it under the new houses.

route.label: Go down into the lower town ahead of the white, door to door, with Iona's drivers

success.narrate: You go down into the lower town at first light, street by street, with Iona's drivers, knocking, telling people what the reeve said: that the walls are open to everyone, to bring what they can carry, and that the carts will come for the rest. By noon half the doors are open.

failure.narrate: You go down into the lower town at first light and knock, and the lower town has heard it all before: the reeve's no, the Hall's offer, the council's letter. Most doors stay shut. A man at the tannery tells you he was born in that house and he will die in it if it comes to that, and shuts the door.

direct.label: Go down into the lower town and start at the first door
direct.text: You go down into the lower town and start knocking at the first door you come to.

approach.narrate: By the afternoon the white is two miles off. You can see it from the bridge: a slow wall of it filling the valley, with the fields going grey under its edge, and the hedges standing up out of it, and then not.
Iona's eleven carts are drawn up in the lower town's square by the fulling mill, with their drivers. Brede is on the old wall above the north gate, watching.

approach.text: Everyone inside who'll come. That's all I said. I'll not drag anyone. That's the same as selling them, only slower.

approach.narrate: At the north gate the Hall's recruiters have packed up their awning. Saul Pruett has not. He is sitting at his table alone, waiting.

crisis.narrate: The white comes up the valley at dusk, faster than anyone thought it could. It takes the far fields first, then the hedges, and then it is in the first street of the lower town, and there are shapes in it.

They are the shapes of what the lower town has forgotten, three hundred years of it: a mill that is not there, a street with another name, people in old coats going about errands nobody remembers. They walk up the lower town's streets as if they lived there, and every house they pass goes cold.
Half the lower town is still in its houses. Eleven carts. Four streets. Not enough time.

crisis.text: Every cart, now! Never mind what they're carrying, put people in them!
Ansel Wick's still in his house by the mill. He won't come out. Someone's got to—

crisis.narrate: Ansel Wick's house, by the fulling mill, has its door shut and its lamp lit. He has not come out.

peaceful.label: Move the lower town's people inside the walls before the white arrives, cart by cart

success.narrate: You know where the old wall's line runs under the new houses: the rolls showed you. The white will come up the lower town as far as that line, because that is the edge of what was given. So you do not try to save the lower town. You empty it, from the bottom up, and you have until the line.

You run the carts. You go door to door ahead of them, getting people out and onto the carts with whatever is in their hands: a cradle, a ham, a cat in a basket, a fiddle. Each cart goes up the hill to the gate full and comes back empty. Iona stands at the gate with her ledger and counts every one of them in, and calls out the number so that you can hear it down below. Four hundred. Six hundred. Nine hundred and ten.

success.text: Last street. I've got the end. Go.

success.narrate: Ansel Wick comes out of his house by the fulling mill on his own, before you reach it, with his lamp in his hand and his coat on, and gets onto the last cart without a word.

The north gate shuts behind the last cart with the white in the street below it. Iona's number at the gate is one thousand and ninety-four. Six would not come. Brede has their names. She says she knew them all, and that every one of them was exactly as stubborn as she is.

failure.narrate: You run the carts, but the shapes are in the second street before the first cart is full, and they are between you and the gate. There is no more getting round them. You will have to go through.

objective.name: Keep the carts moving
objective.label: Keep the shapes off the carts to the north gate
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the shapes off the carts long enough to get the lower town's people up the hill to the north gate.
objective.failText: The last two carts do not reach the gate. Their people come in on foot through the white, holding hands in a line, grey to the shoulder, and some of them cannot tell you their own street when you ask. Iona's number at the gate is nine hundred and sixty.
objective.successText: The last cart goes in through the north gate with the white at its wheels, and the gate shuts behind it.

b3-ashford.retainerName: Shape of the Old Lower Town

oneOf.narrate: Morning on the old wall. The white lies in the lower town exactly to the line of the old foundations, as if somebody had drawn it there. Above the line is the upper town, crammed with four thousand people and eleven hundred more, steaming in the cold. Below it is the lower town: its houses, its tannery, its mill, its fields, all grey and still.

Morning on the old wall. The white lies in the lower town to the line of the old foundations. Above the line the upper town is crammed full. Below it the lower town lies grey and still, and in its second street are two of Iona's carts, overturned, where the fight was.

after.narrate: The white has not come over the line. It has not gone back, either. It is waiting, the way it must have waited three hundred years ago, for the town to decide.

after.text: Well. Now we find out what our no costs. All winter, with eleven hundred more mouths, and no wood, and that at the foot of the hill.

after.narrate: At the north gate Saul Pruett is still at his table. Ansel Wick is standing in front of it, in his coat, with his hat in his hands. He has been standing there since dawn. He has asked Brede's leave, at the gate, in front of everyone, to give himself to the Hall's bell so that the white will go back down the valley. Brede has not answered him.
Brede has the old wall's building rolls under her arm, with the word given beside every street.

A rider from Highpass came in the night: Highpass will take the children of any town in the valley, if they are brought. Brede read it out in the market at dawn. The town meeting voted it down by a show of hands. Ashford's children stay with Ashford.

after.text: Nobody persuades me. I told you that. So don't. Tell me what you'd do, and then I'll do what I do.

decisions.label: Back Ashford's no: everyone inside the walls, and the lower town given up
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Ashford keeps its no. The lower town's houses and fields are lost to the white; its people are inside the walls.
